en.description: Breeschoten has belonged to the former Lordship of Scherpenzeel since the end of the nineteenth century. The name refers to ’schoten’, derived from the Germanic ’skautum’: a higher, wooded corner of sandy ground jutting into marshy terrain. Until the early twentieth century it was a marshy heath field with seepage sites; only around 1930 was the last part reclaimed, with conifers planted for pit props in the coal mines. In the small-scale landscape lies the Breeschoterplas, a seepage-water fen further excavated in 1915 for duck hunting. Around it lie farms with names such as Ubbeschoten, Veenschoten and Kolfschoten. The Breeschoterpad, a klompenpad, leads through this hedgerow landscape.

en.location: 📍 Renswoude, Renswoude municipality · Castle wood · c. 60 ha
en.description: Around Kasteel Renswoude — dating from 1654 on the spot where the fortified house Borchwal had stood since the late fourteenth century — lies a 60-hectare castle wood with broadleaf trees over 150 years old. In front of the castle stretches the Grand Canal, a moat of no less than 700 metres dug around 1700. The park originally had the Dutch classicist style, received the geometric French baroque style with straight avenues in 1708, and changed in the early nineteenth century to the English landscape style with flowing lines around the castle pond. At a fork in the castle wood stand three monumental Italian benches of 1900. Behind the castle lies a park with beeches, oaks, a pond and a dovecote. The wood links to the Grebbelinie.

Langs de groene dijk liggen onder meer Fort aan de Buursteeg (1786, met bezoekerscentrum), Fort Daatselaar (1799), de Asschatterkade en de Post van Lambalgen.

tags: Water line · 18th-century line with forts and green dikes
en.location: 📍 Renswoude–Veenendaal–Scherpenzeel, Utrecht/Gelderland border · Water line · over 40 km of green heritage
en.description: The Grebbelinie is a water line on the border of Gelderland and Utrecht, laid out in the eighteenth century and over 40 kilometres long: from the Grebbeberg to the former Zuiderzee, straight through the Gelderse Vallei. By flooding the low land (inundation) the enemy’s passage was blocked. The line was brought into position again in 1939–40 under the name Valleistelling as the main defence, after which heavy fighting took place in May 1940. In 1951 the line was finally abolished; since 1976 it has been a nature reserve largely managed by Staatsbosbeheer, and since 2011 a national monument. Along the green dike lie, among others, Fort aan de Buursteeg (1786, with visitor centre), Fort Daatselaar (1799), the Asschatterkade and the Post van Lambalgen.

en.location: 📍 Cothen, Wijk bij Duurstede municipality · Knightly manor · Langbroekerdijk
en.description: Castle Hardenbroek lies along the historic Langbroekerwetering, in the castle belt between Cothen and Werkhoven. The name means hard clay soil on a broek (marshland). The castle was founded around 1280–1300 by the Van Wulven family as a square keep and was first mentioned in 1392; in 1536 it was recognised as a knightly manor. The Van Hardenbroek family remained owner until 1684. In 1762 Johan Adolph van Hardenbroek had the courtyard built over with a prestigious building with tower-shaped corner pavilions; the rear facade of 1793 is attributed to Jacob Otten Husly. The estate of some 60 hectares comprises woodland, farmland and a park in English landscape style. The castle is privately occupied and clearly visible from the public road.

en.description: The Leeuwenburgh country seat lies on the Langbroekerwetering, west of the village of Langbroek. The moated, block-shaped house was built in 1657 by Christiaan van Vianen for the Utrecht patrician Gerard Zoudenbalch — and was accordingly first called Zoudenbalch; in 1667 the new owner Melchior Toussain renamed it Leeuwenburgh. Around 1700 Gideon Boudaan had a park laid out in French classical style with a round basin and sightlines, the structure of which remains. In 1859 Pieter de Beaufort had the house largely rebuilt, the moat being filled in to form a pond with a small island. The wooden dovecote (1880) and the sightlines to tower and farm are characteristic. The De Beaufort family is still the owner.

The house is privately occupied; the avenues and surrounding woodland are partly accessible and link to the Kaapse Bossen.

en.description: The Kaapse Bossen on the Utrechtse Heuvelrug near Doorn owe their name to the eighteenth-century landowner Hendrik Swellengrebel, governor of the Cape Colony, for whom the rolling woodland reminded him of Table Mountain. Swellengrebel had the first trees planted there in 1823. In 1904 Natuurmonumenten bought the woods as its first property on the ridge. Highlights are the Doornse Kei, a boulder from the ice age, the Stenen Tafel (stone table), the 25-metre-high De Kaap lookout tower with views over the treetops, and Chalet Helenaheuvel. The woods also contain prehistoric burial mounds. The area links to the Ruiterberg estate and borders the Moersbergen estate.

nl.description: Bij Leersum, op de zuidflank van de Utrechtse Heuvelrug, ligt de Darthuizerberg, genoemd naar de oude ridderhofstad Darthuizen die ooit aan de voet van de heuvel stond. Het reliëfrijke terrein is gevormd door de Darthuizerpoort, een smeltwaterdal uit de voorlaatste ijstijd dat de stuwwal hier doorsnijdt. en.location: 📍 Leersum, Utrechtse Heuvelrug municipality · Woodland and heath · Darthuizerberg
en.description: Near Leersum, on the southern flank of the Utrechtse Heuvelrug, lies the Darthuizerberg, named after the old knightly manor Darthuizen that once stood at the foot of the hill. The rolling terrain was shaped by the Darthuizerpoort, a meltwater valley from the penultimate ice age that cuts through the push moraine here. On the hilltop lies the Donderberg, from where you look out over the Gelderse Vallei. The area is a mixture of coniferous and broadleaf woodland, heath and sand paths, and runs over into the Dartheide and the ski-slope area. Immediately to the south lies the Broekhuizen estate. The height differences make this a popular walking area with panoramas.

The estate near Leersum lies in a patchwork of country seats — Broekhuizen, La Licorne, De Kleine Hoogstraat and Burnakker — with a variety of woodland, avenues, meadows and ponds. The name refers to the former Voreneng farm. The Stichtse Lustwarande is characterised by monumental avenue trees, rhododendron woods and sightlines from the hills over the Gelderse Vallei. It is a popular walking area with a long estate history.

nl.description: De Grote Maat is een omgracht landgoed aan de rand van Cothen, verbonden met kasteel Noortwijck aan de overzijde van de weg. De versterkte boerderij stamt uit de 14e eeuw; in 1699 brandde het huis af en in 1722 werd het herbouwd. Het terrein van zo’n 52 tot 68 hectare bestaat uit weilanden, boomgaarden, houtwallen en een gracht met oude bomen. Er loopt een discussie over natuurinclusieve landbouw op het terrein. Het landgoed is particulier, maar de omgeving leent zich goed voor een wandeling langs de Kromme Rijn.

en.location: 📍 Cothen, Wijk bij Duurstede municipality · Estate · De Grote Maat
en.description: De Grote Maat is a moated estate on the edge of Cothen, linked to castle Noortwijck across the road. The fortified farm dates from the 14th century; in 1699 the house burned down and in 1722 it was rebuilt. The site of some 52 to 68 hectares consists of meadows, orchards, hedge banks and a moat with old trees. The estate lies on the edge of the floodplain of the Kromme Rijn region, where wet grassland and small-scale farming alternate. There is a discussion about nature-inclusive agriculture on the site. The estate is private, but the surroundings lend themselves well to a walk along the Kromme Rijn.

Het oorspronkelijke huis ging in 1906 door brand verloren en werd daarna herbouwd. Het landgoed omvat naast Broekhuizen ook het huis ’t Lage Laer, met park, lanen, weilanden en bos. Het landgoed is particulier bewoond, maar de lanen en de Donderberg zijn geliefde wandelplekken en sluiten aan op de Darthuizerberg.

en.description: Broekhuizen near Leersum is an old knightly manor at the foot of the Donderberg, on the transition from the Utrechtse Heuvelrug to the Gelderse Vallei. The original house was lost to fire in 1906 and rebuilt afterwards. Besides Broekhuizen the estate also includes the house ’t Lage Laer, with park, avenues, meadows and woodland. The Donderberg is a striking hill with views over the valley, which the estate shares with the adjacent Dartheide. The estate is privately occupied, but the avenues and the Donderberg are popular walking spots and link to the Darthuizerberg.

tags: Bos en heide · Utrechts Landschap met hakhout en skibaan
nl.location: 📍 Leersum, gemeente Utrechtse Heuvelrug · Bos en heide · Utrechts Landschap
nl.description: Breeveen en Dartheide zijn twee naast elkaar gelegen terreinen van het Utrechts Landschap op de zuidflank van de Heuvelrug bij Leersum. Breeveen was van oorsprong een natte heide, werd in de oorlogsjaren gebruikt als militair oefenterrein en raakte daarna zwaar verwaarloosd. In 1960 kocht de familie Pierson het terrein, herstelde de heide en droeg het in 1961 over aan het Utrechts Landschap. Dartheide is een oud landgoed met monumentaal hakhout van beuk en eik en de bekende skibaan, die als hellingbos en open terrein bijzonder is voor planten en insecten. De terreinen lopen over in de Darthuizerberg en het Leersumse Veld.

tags: Woodland and heath · Utrechts Landschap with coppice and ski slope
en.location: 📍 Leersum, Utrechtse Heuvelrug municipality · Woodland and heath · Utrechts Landschap
en.description: Breeveen and Dartheide are two adjacent Utrechts Landschap sites on the southern flank of the ridge near Leersum. Breeveen was originally wet heath, was used as a military training ground during the war years and then fell into serious neglect. In 1960 the Pierson family bought the site, restored the heath and transferred it to the Utrechts Landschap in 1961. Dartheide is an old estate with monumental coppice of beech and oak and the well-known ski slope, which as a slope woodland and open ground is special for plants and insects. The sites run over into the Darthuizerberg and the Leersumse Veld.
